title: Staying in Work Best for Brain Health — Study
paragraphs: Many people dream of retiring early so that they can relax and enjoy their free time. However, new research from the United States suggests that leaving work too soon may come at a cost to the brain.

The research was carried out by economists Noah Arman Kouchekinia and David Neumark and public health researcher Tim Bruckner, all of the University of California, Irvine. Their findings were published in May 2026 as a working paper by the National Bureau of Economic Research, which means that it has not yet been through the full peer review process that most scientific studies go through.

The researchers used data from the Health and Retirement Study, a long-running study run by the University of Michigan that has tracked the cognitive abilities of around 40,000 Americans over many years. They focused on people aged between 51 and 75.

Previous studies had already found a link between early retirement and faster cognitive decline. However, it was difficult to know whether leaving work actually caused this decline. After all, cognitive problems themselves can make it harder for people to keep their jobs, which could explain the connection. Other factors, such as depression, could also affect both employment and thinking skills.

To get around this problem, the researchers looked at what happened when large numbers of jobs suddenly disappeared in the areas where older people lived. Because these job losses were caused by changes in the local economy, rather than by people's own health, the researchers were able to get a clearer picture of the effect of work itself.

The results showed that people's scores on cognitive tests dropped significantly after these job losses. In other words, leaving employment led to cognitive decline, while people who stayed in work tended to keep their thinking skills for longer. The effects were mainly seen among men aged 51 to 64.
Experts believe that work keeps the brain active by providing regular mental challenges and social contact.

Neumark pointed out that cognitive decline is very expensive for society. However, the researchers stressed that the findings do not mean that people should never retire, or that they should stay in an unhealthy work environment.
